title: The salt farmers of the coast
paragraphs: Along parts of the Indonesian coast, families still make salt in much the same way as their grandparents did. During the dry season, they let sea water into shallow, flat ponds near the shore. The ponds are lined with packed clay so that the water does not soak away. The sun and wind slowly remove the water. As the liquid becomes stronger, it is moved from pond to pond until white crystals finally form on the surface. The crystals are then raked into piles, left to dry and carried to a store near the road.

The work looks simple, but it demands good judgement. If a farmer moves the water too early, the crystals will be small and dirty. If it is moved too late, a hard crust can form that is difficult to rake. If rain falls at the wrong moment, several weeks of work can disappear in an afternoon. Older farmers often read the sky and the feel of the wind before they decide what to do, and they pass this knowledge on to their children by working beside them.

In recent years, this way of life has come under pressure. Cheaper salt is brought in from countries where large machines do most of the work. Longer wet seasons have also shortened the time available for drying. As a result, many young people now prefer jobs in the cities, where the income is steadier.

However, some farmers have found a way to continue. They have formed small groups that sell directly to restaurants and food shops, and they describe how their salt is made on each packet. Customers are often willing to pay more when they know where a product comes from. Some groups also invite visitors to watch the salt being raked at harvest time. This does not solve every problem, and a poor season can still be very hard. Even so, it has given some families a reason to stay, and a few of their children have returned from the cities to learn the work.
